name: Fela Kuti
hook: The Lagos bandleader who, with Tony Allen, made Afrobeat out of highlife, jazz and James Brown's funk, and whose songs against the military government got his home burned down.
blurb: Fela Kuti was born in Abeokuta, Nigeria, in 1938, the son of the feminist activist Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti. He studied music at Trinity College of Music in London from 1958, then led bands in Lagos, playing a mix of highlife and jazz without much success. In 1969 he stayed in Los Angeles, where Sandra Izsadore introduced him to Black Power writing, and he heard James Brown's funk. It changed his politics and his music. With his drummer Tony Allen he created Afrobeat out of Yoruba music, highlife, jazz and funk: long songs with interlocking guitars, horns and a drum pattern that never stops, sung in Nigerian Pidgin so it could travel across Africa. His lyrics attacked Nigeria's military rulers. His 1976 album 'Zombie' mocked soldiers for blindly obeying orders, and in 1977 about a thousand soldiers attacked his home, the Kalakuta Republic, burned it, destroyed his studio and tapes, and threw his mother from a window. She died of her injuries, and he carried her coffin to the main army barracks in Lagos. He died in 1997 of complications from AIDS, having publicly denied the disease.
